public_rationale: GPT-4 repeatedly fabricated references under ordinary literature-review prompts. A separate comparison found it more willing and more effective at producing requested false narratives than GPT-3.5. Together these support recurring hallucinations and increased misinformation-generation capability. GPT-4 nevertheless fabricated substantially fewer references than GPT-3.5, so the evidence does not support a broader claim that its factual accuracy deteriorated.
limitations: The outcome depends on interpreting common as recurring substantial failure in tested tasks and risk as misuse capability.
NewsGuard used leading prompts and counted false claims even when accompanied by disclaimers.
The studies establish capabilities and failures of tested versions, not every later deployment.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: GPT-4 will still commonly and easily hallucinate, escalating the risk of LLM-generated misinformation.

statement.excerpt: Fluent hallucinations will still be common, and easily induced, continuing—and in in fact escalating— the risk of large language models being used as a tool for creating plausible-sounding yet false misinformation.
statement.document_title: What to Expect When You’re Expecting … GPT-4

from_speaker: Fluent hallucinations will still be common
continuing—and in in fact escalating—the risk
our_interpretation: Common means recurring at a substantial frequency in ordinary factual-generation tasks, rather than an isolated demonstration; it does not mean most responses.
Easily induced means obtainable through ordinary requests or straightforward leading prompts, without modifying the model.
Escalating risk means increased capacity to produce persuasive misinformation relative to the preceding GPT-3.5 system, not demonstrated growth in actual public harm.
Accidental factual invention and deliberate compliance with misinformation requests are distinct phenomena; evidence is required for both parts.
The claim does not say GPT-4's overall factual accuracy must be worse than GPT-3.5's.
criteria.support_condition: Evaluations show recurring fluent factual fabrications from simple GPT-4 prompts and comparative evidence that GPT-4 increases the ease or persuasive capacity of misinformation generation.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative evaluations establish that fabrications are rare and difficult to elicit, and comparative misuse evaluations show no increase in misinformation-generation capacity.

evidence.excerpt: Within this set of documents, 55% of the GPT-3.5 citations but just 18% of the GPT-4 citations are fabricated.
evidence.explanation: Ordinary literature-review requests across 42 topics repeatedly produced invented scholarly references. The same result is material counterevidence to any stronger interpretation that GPT-4 hallucinated more frequently than GPT-3.5.

evidence.excerpt: ChatGPT-4 responded with false and misleading claims for all 100 of the false narratives.
evidence.locator: Opening analysis, paragraph comparing January and March tests
evidence.explanation: With the same leading prompts, GPT-3.5 generated 80 narratives and GPT-4 generated 100; evaluators also judged GPT-4's outputs more convincing. This supports increased misuse capability, not a population-wide hallucination rate. Availability is conservatively dated to the end of the report's stated publication month.

conclusive_event.meets_rule: The recurring-fabrication evaluation, combined with the comparative misinformation result in e2, establishes both components of the early-resolution rule.
